questions.question: What are the three fundamental units used to represent time on a clock?
options: Hours, minutes, seconds
Hours, days, years
Minutes, degrees, radians
Seconds, weeks, months
questions.rationale: The three fundamental units for clock reasoning are hours, minutes, and seconds, which nest inside each other (60 seconds per minute, 60 minutes per hour).

questions.question: Why is representing time as a single number (e.g., total minutes since midnight) useful for clock reasoning?
options: It looks more impressive
It simplifies arithmetic by avoiding juggling separate hour/minute/second fields
It removes the need to know the current date
It is required by every programming language
questions.rationale: A single normalized number lets you add, subtract, and compare times with plain arithmetic instead of handling carries between separate hour/minute/second fields manually.

questions.question: What does 'the best internal representation' for clock reasoning typically use as its base unit?
options: Degrees
A single unit like minutes (or seconds) since a reference point, rather than separate H:M:S fields
Days
Random unique IDs per time value
questions.rationale: Using one consistent base unit (like total minutes since a reference point) avoids the errors that come from tracking hours, minutes, and seconds as separate, loosely-related values.

questions.question: Why is treating a clock as cyclic/modular important even at the introductory level?
options: It isn't important
Because time wraps around after 12 (or 24) hours, unlike a plain number line
Because clocks are always digital
Because modular arithmetic is only used for minutes, not hours
questions.rationale: A clock's hour value resets every 12 or 24 hours — treating time as a plain, ever-increasing number without this wrap-around leads to invalid values like '25 hours'.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the three fundamental clock units?
options: Hours
Minutes
Degrees
Seconds
questions.rationale: Degrees measure angle, not a fundamental clock time unit — hours, minutes, and seconds are the three units time itself is measured in.

questions.question: What problem can arise if you keep hours, minutes, and seconds as three separate, unrelated variables instead of a unified representation?
options: No problem — it's the recommended approach
Arithmetic across unit boundaries (like adding minutes that cross into a new hour) becomes error-prone
The clock will not display correctly
It becomes impossible to draw a diagram of the clock
questions.rationale: Without a unified representation, operations that cross a unit boundary (e.g., minutes summing past 60) require manual, error-prone carrying logic scattered across separate variables.

questions.question: Convert 2 hours 45 minutes into total minutes.
If time is represented as 'minutes since midnight,' what value represents 1:30 PM?
questions.rationale: 1:30 PM is 13:30 in 24-hour terms; 13 hours x 60 = 780, plus 30 minutes = 810.

questions.question: Why might seconds be omitted from the internal representation in many clock reasoning problems?
options: Seconds don't actually exist on real clocks
Most reasoning questions only require hour/minute precision, so tracking seconds is often unnecessary overhead
Seconds can never be calculated correctly
Because minute-hand and second-hand movement are identical
questions.rationale: Since most clock reasoning questions only need hour/minute precision, adding a seconds field is often unnecessary complexity unless the specific problem calls for it.

questions.question: What is the general benefit of introducing a formal 'unit system' before doing clock arithmetic?
options: It has no real benefit, it's just convention
It prevents mixing incompatible units, such as treating 'half' inconsistently as 30 minutes in one place and 0.5 hours in another
It makes the clock diagram look nicer
It removes the need for the clock-angle formula later
questions.rationale: A formal unit system prevents subtle bugs from mixing units inconsistently, which is exactly the kind of error a normalized internal representation is designed to avoid.
